description: AgriX SIH Demo/Prototype Crop-Aware Disease Catalog

diseases.overview: Early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It targets older foliage first and creates characteristic target-board lesions, eventually defoliating the lower plant canopy.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots on older lower leaves.
Concentric rings forming a 'target-board' or bullseye pattern within leaf spots.
Yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf tissue surrounding the necrotic spots.
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions on tomato stems and fruit near the stem end.
immediate_actions: Prune off heavily infected lower leaves during dry afternoon hours.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation to keep tomato foliage dry.
Mulch soil around the base of plants to prevent soil-borne fungal spores from splashing onto leaves.
Dispose of removed infected foliage away from the field; do not compost.
prevention: Practice 2- to 3-year crop rotation avoiding other solanaceous crops (potato, pepper, eggplant).
Ensure adequate plant spacing (60 cm) and stake plants for maximum air circulation.
Plant certified disease-free transplants and resistant cultivars when available.
monitoring: Scout lower leaves twice weekly during warm, humid weather (24-29°C).
Check for rapid upward progression of leaf spots after rain or irrigation.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or extension office if concentric lesions spread past the lower third of the plant canopy.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Late blight, caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, is a destructive, fast-spreading disease that causes rapid water-soaking of foliage, white fuzzy growth, and rotting fruit in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked pale green or dark brown lesions on leaves.
White fuzzy fungal-like sporulation visible on the underside of leaves in moist morning conditions.
Dark brown, greasy-looking lesions on stems and petioles.
Firm, brown, leathery rot spreading over green and ripe tomato fruit.
immediate_actions: Immediately pull and bag severely infected plants to halt rapid spore dispersal.
Cease all sprinkler or overhead irrigation immediately.
Ensure field drainage is clear so standing water does not linger.
prevention: Plant certified late-blight resistant tomato varieties.
Space rows widely to promote rapid foliage drying after morning dew or rain.
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to potato fields.
monitoring: Scout canopy daily during prolonged cool, cloudy, and wet periods (15-22°C).
Inspect leaf undersides in early morning for white sporulation.
diseases.expert_escalation: Immediately alert local agricultural extension or KVK if late blight symptoms appear, as late blight can destroy whole fields within days.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Tomato leaf curl virus is a severe viral disease transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). It stunts plants, curls leaves upward and inward, and severely restricts fruit set.
symptoms: Severe upward and inward curling, puckering, and reduction in leaf size.
Prominent interveinal chlorosis (yellowing) and thickening of leaf veins.
Marked stunting of plants with shortened internodes producing a bushy habit.
Excessive flower dropping with minimal to no harvestable fruit formation.
immediate_actions: Rogue out and bury severely infected young plants immediately.
Install yellow sticky traps (15-20 per acre) across the field to monitor and trap vector whiteflies.
Remove alternate weed hosts (Parthenium, Datura) along field borders.
prevention: Plant leaf-curl-resistant tomato hybrids recommended for your region.
Raise seedlings inside 40-50 mesh insect-proof nylon net nurseries.
Grow 2-3 border rows of tall barrier crops like maize or sorghum.
monitoring: Scout leaf undersides in early morning for whitefly populations.
Inspect new vegetative flushes weekly for early vein clearing and curling.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact your local KVK for integrated vector management if whitefly counts exceed economic thresholds.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas spp.) produces small, dark angular water-soaked specks on leaves and scabby raised pustules on tomato fruit, leading to severe defoliation during rainy periods.
symptoms: Small (2-3 mm), dark brown, water-soaked angular spots on leaves.
Spots developing yellow halos, coalescing, and causing leaf browning and drop.
Small, raised, scab-like rough black lesions on green fruit surfaces.
immediate_actions: Never work, prune, or harvest in tomato fields when foliage is wet.
Switch to drip or furrow irrigation to eliminate splash dispersal.
Remove and destroy severely spotted lower leaves during dry, sunny weather.
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds treated with hot water (50°C for 25 min).
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for at least two years.
Disinfect pruning tools and stakes with 70% alcohol.
monitoring: Inspect transplants in nursery beds before planting in the field.
Scout lower leaf canopy following stormy, wind-driven rains.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult local KVK horticultural officers if bacterial spots spread to the top canopy.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici) is a persistent soil-borne fungal disease that blocks water-conducting xylem vessels, causing progressive one-sided yellowing and wilting.
symptoms: Yellowing of lower leaves, often starting on one side of the plant or leaf ('yellow flag').
Wilting of foliage during warm daytime hours with night recovery in early stages.
Distinct dark brown vascular ring discoloration visible when stem is cut lengthwise.
Complete plant stunting, permanent wilting, and plant death.
immediate_actions: Uproot and destroy infected plants with their root systems to reduce soil inoculum.
Do not irrigate through wilt-affected patches to prevent spreading spores.
Disinfect farm implements and footwear after working in affected areas.
prevention: Plant Fusarium-resistant tomato cultivars (labeled 'F' or 'FF').
Practice long-term crop rotation (3-4 years) with non-host crops like maize or paddy.
Enrich soil with Trichoderma-amended well-decomposed organic manure.
monitoring: Scout fields during warm afternoon hours when transpiration stress is highest (27-32°C).
Split stems of wilting plants longitudinally to inspect for brown vascular streaking.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact local extension specialists for soil health analysis and bio-control recommendations.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Anthracnose and fruit rot (Colletotrichum capsici) is a damaging fungal disease that produces sunken circular rot lesions with concentric rings on chilli pods and dieback of twigs.
symptoms: Circular or oblong sunken necrotic spots on ripening red and green pods.
Concentric rings of tiny black fruiting specks (acervuli) inside the fruit lesions.
Dieback of tender branches from top downward with straw-colored dried twigs.
Premature shedding of diseased pods and flowers.
immediate_actions: Collect and destroy all fallen and spotted pods from the field.
Prune dead twigs 2-3 cm below the discoloration line using sanitized shears.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; switch to drip or furrow.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds treated with biocontrol or approved seed treatments.
Maintain adequate spacing (60 x 45 cm) for good canopy aeration.
Rotate crops with non-solanaceous species like pulses or cereals.
monitoring: Scout pods closely during fruit development and ripening in humid weather.
Inspect upper shoot tips for early signs of twig drying.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult local KVK horticultural specialists if fruit rot affects more than 10% of harvestable pods.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Chilli leaf curl virus is transmitted by whiteflies and thrips, causing severe upward and downward leaf curling, puckering, vein thickening, and stunted bushy growth.
symptoms: Upward and downward curling, puckering, and size reduction of young leaves.
Thickening of leaf veins with chlorotic yellow mottling.
Shortened internodes resulting in a stunted, bushy 'rosette' habit.
Malformed, small, wrinkled pods with poor seed development.
immediate_actions: Rogue and bury severely curled young plants immediately.
Set up yellow sticky traps (15-20 per acre) to trap vectoring whiteflies and thrips.
Remove weed hosts (Solanum nigrum, Parthenium) around field borders.
prevention: Grow chilli seedlings under insect-proof nursery mesh nets.
Plant border barrier rows of tall crops like maize, sorghum, or pearl millet.
Select leaf-curl tolerant chilli cultivars recommended by local research institutes.
monitoring: Scout the underside of top young leaves for whiteflies and thrips with a hand lens.
Check weekly for early puckering on growing shoot tips.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact local KVK extension officers for integrated vector management protocols.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Powdery mildew (Leveillula taurica) causes white powdery fungal patches on the underside of leaves with corresponding yellow patches on the upper surface, causing severe defoliation.
symptoms: White powdery fungal patches developing on lower leaf surfaces.
Corresponding bright yellow chlorotic patches on upper leaf surfaces.
Down-rolling of leaf margins followed by extensive premature leaf drop.
Sunscald on exposed fruits due to loss of protective canopy foliage.
immediate_actions: Prune off severely affected lower leaves to improve airflow through the canopy.
Ensure field is not moisture-stressed, as dry soil accelerates mildew defoliation.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which produces dense, succulent foliage.
prevention: Adopt wider row spacing to facilitate sunlight penetration into the inner canopy.
Practice crop sanitation by destroying post-harvest plant debris.
Plant tolerant chilli varieties in mildew-endemic regions.
monitoring: Scout lower canopy leaves during cool, dry days with warm humid nights.
Inspect leaf undersides for initial faint white mycelial growth.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact extension staff if powdery mildew symptoms advance to the middle canopy.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Bacterial leaf spot (Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria) produces small water-soaked dark spots on leaves and fruit, causing heavy leaf shedding.
symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaves turning dark brown with pale centers.
Yellow halo encircling older leaf lesions.
Severe defoliation giving plants a bare, leggy appearance.
Small, rough, raised wart-like brown spots on chilli fruit surfaces.
immediate_actions: Never enter or cultivate chilli fields while plants are wet with dew or rain.
Switch immediately to ground or drip irrigation.
Collect and destroy fallen diseased leaves from under the canopy.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and soak seeds in warm water (50°C for 25 min) before sowing.
Rotate fields with non-host crops (maize, sorghum, rice) for at least two seasons.
Avoid field operations when rain is forecasted.
monitoring: Check seedlings in the nursery bed for small angular dark specks.
Scout field after strong wind-driven rains.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult local KVK for verified bactericidal management if spots spread rapidly.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum) is a destructive soil-borne fungus that invades vascular bundles, causing leaf yellowing, drooping, and plant death.
symptoms: Gradual yellowing and upward curling of lower leaves progressing upward.
Wilting of foliage during daytime with temporary recovery in cool night hours.
Dark brown vascular ring discoloration visible when the base of the stem is cut open.
Decay of feeder roots and eventual complete drying of the plant.
immediate_actions: Uproot and destroy infected plants with their root balls to restrict spread in the soil.
Avoid moving wet soil from affected patches to healthy parts of the field.
Regulate irrigation to prevent water stagnation around plant crowns.
prevention: Practice crop rotation (3-4 years) with cereals or marigold to suppress Fusarium inoculum.
Incorporate organic bio-agents (Trichoderma viride) with well-rotted FYM at land preparation.
Plant chilli crops on raised beds with good subsoil drainage.
monitoring: Scout fields during warm weather (28-32°C) following irrigation cycles.
Examine stem cross-sections of wilting plants for brown vascular rings.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult KVK specialists for soil treatment and bio-control recommendations in wilt-affected soils.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae) is a major fungal disease causing spindle- or diamond-shaped lesions on leaves, neck rot of panicles, and severe yield loss.
symptoms: Spindle- or diamond-shaped lesions with grey or whitish centers and brown margins on leaves.
Lesions coalescing to dry up and kill entire leaf blades.
Blackened, shriveled panicle neck ('neck blast') causing panicles to break and fall over.
Blanked or partially filled grains with brown discoloration.
immediate_actions: Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogen fertilizers; split nitrogen into smaller doses.
Maintain a steady 2-5 cm water layer in the paddy field to suppress blast development.
Remove weed hosts (Echinochloa, Leersia) on bunds that harbor blast spores.
prevention: Sow blast-resistant certified paddy varieties suited for your agro-climatic zone.
Treat seeds before sowing with recommended bio-control or certified fungicide formulations.
Avoid late planting and staggered planting in adjacent plots.
monitoring: Scout nursery and tillering stages during cloudy days with high relative humidity (>90%) and night dew.
Check top leaves and panicle neck node closely at heading stage.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact local KVK or agricultural officer immediately if neck blast symptoms appear during panicle emergence.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Bacterial leaf blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae) is a widespread vascular bacterial disease causing wavy yellow-white lesions along leaf margins from tip downwards.
symptoms: Water-soaked stripes starting from leaf tips and margins, expanding into wavy yellowish-white stripes.
Milky bacterial ooze droplets appearing on young lesions in humid morning hours.
Leaves rolling, turning straw-colored, and dying prematurely.
'Kresek' or total seedling wilt phase in young transplants within 2-3 weeks.
immediate_actions: Drain standing water from the field for 2-3 days if blight is spreading rapidly.
Suspend top-dressing of nitrogen fertilizer until disease progression ceases.
Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplanting as wounds allow bacterial entry.
prevention: Plant certified blight-resistant rice cultivars.
Apply balanced potash (K) fertilizers to enhance plant cell wall resistance.
Keep irrigation channels clean and prevent floodwater transfer between adjacent fields.
monitoring: Scout fields during active tillering to panicle initiation stages following cyclones or heavy winds.
Check leaf margins for characteristic wavy, serrated yellow borders.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult local KVK extension agronomists if bacterial blight exceeds 15% of the leaf canopy.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Brown spot (Bipolaris oryzae) is a fungal disease closely linked with soil nutrient deficiency, producing thousands of small oval dark brown spots on leaves and glumes.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval dark brown spots scattered across leaf blades.
Mature spots with grey or light brown centers surrounded by a distinct dark reddish-brown margin and yellow halo.
Discoloration and black spotting of grains on the panicle ('pecky rice').
Seedling blight and poor germination when infected seeds are sown.
immediate_actions: Top-dress with balanced potassium and micronutrients (zinc, silica) to boost plant vigor.
Ensure fields do not suffer drought or intermittent water stress.
Avoid planting in severely nutrient-depleted, unamended sandy soils.
prevention: Treat seeds before sowing with hot water (52-54°C for 10 min) or approved seed dressings.
Conduct soil testing and apply balanced N-P-K along with farmyard manure.
Destroy infected crop stubble and wild grass hosts on bunds.
monitoring: Scout seedlings in nurseries and plants at maximum tillering to grain filling.
Monitor light-textured or unfertilized plots where soil nutrient stress is highest.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult KVK specialists for soil nutrient correction and integrated disease management.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Sheath blight (Rhizoctonia solani) produces large oval or snake-skin lesions on leaf sheaths near the waterline that creep upward to choke upper leaves and panicles.
symptoms: Oval or irregular greenish-grey water-soaked spots on leaf sheaths just above the water line.
Lesions enlarging with bleached white/grey centers and dark reddish-brown borders (snake-skin appearance).
Infection creeping up to upper sheaths and flag leaves causing premature lodging.
Tiny spherical brown fungal resting bodies (sclerotia) loosely attached to diseased sheaths.
immediate_actions: Drain excess floodwater and practice alternate wetting and moderate drying to aerate the root zone.
Avoid excessive nitrogen top-dressing which increases canopy humidity and density.
Skim floating sclerotia from standing water after puddling during next land preparation.
prevention: Maintain optimal hill spacing (20 x 15 cm) to avoid excessively dense plant canopies.
Apply potash in split doses along with nitrogen.
Apply Trichoderma-enriched organic compost during basal land preparation.
monitoring: Inspect lower leaf sheaths near the water level from maximum tillering stage onward.
Check dense patches of canopy after humid, cloudy weather.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact local extension agronomists if lesions reach the third leaf from top before heading.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Rice tungro disease is a devastating viral disease complex transmitted by green leafhoppers (Nephotettix virescens). It causes intense plant stunting and bright yellow-orange leaf discoloration.
symptoms: Intense yellowing or orange-yellow discoloration of leaves starting from the tips.
Severe stunting of rice hills with reduced tiller numbers.
Mottled appearance on young leaves with small rusty brown specks.
Delayed flowering, incomplete panicle exertion, and sterile/unfilled grains.
immediate_actions: Rogue and destroy infected hills in early stages to eliminate virus reservoirs.
Set up light traps to monitor and catch vector green leafhoppers at night.
Maintain intermittent drainage to disturb leafhopper habitats.
prevention: Plant tungro-resistant or tolerant paddy cultivars.
Synchronize planting across the village to break the leafhopper reproduction cycle.
Plow under rice stubble immediately after harvest to destroy green leafhopper habitats.
monitoring: Sweep-net nursery beds and young tillering fields weekly to check green leafhopper counts.
Inspect early-stage fields for patchy yellowing and stunted hills.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact local KVK extension officers immediately if green leafhopper counts exceed 1 per hill in young paddy.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Leaf rust (Puccinia triticina) is the most common wheat rust, producing small, round to oval orange-brown powdery pustules scattered randomly on upper leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval bright orange-brown powdery pustules on the upper leaf surface.
Pustules scattered randomly across the leaf blade without forming distinct stripes.
Rubbing leaves with fingers leaves a reddish-brown powdery spore residue.
Premature yellowing and drying of leaves, resulting in shriveled grains.
immediate_actions: Inspect fields immediately to map early focal hotspots of infection.
Avoid late irrigation that raises humidity in dense crop canopies.
Eradicate volunteer wheat plants and alternate hosts around field edges.
prevention: Sow certified rust-resistant wheat varieties recommended for your agro-climatic zone.
Sow crops timely during the recommended sowing window to escape late-season rust buildup.
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen; maintain balanced potassium levels.
monitoring: Scout upper canopy leaves weekly starting from jointing to grain fill stages.
Monitor fields closely when temperatures range between 15-25°C with morning dews.
diseases.expert_escalation: Immediately alert local KVK or Wheat Directorate extension team if rust pustules appear on flag leaves before flowering.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis) thrives in cool climates, forming narrow yellow-orange pustules arranged in parallel linear stripes along the leaf veins.
symptoms: Bright yellow to orange-yellow powdery pustules arranged in distinct parallel stripes along leaf veins.
Linear stripes appearing on leaf blades, leaf sheaths, and even glumes.
Severe chlorosis and necrosis of leaf tissue leading to complete drying.
Drastic reduction in grain number and severe grain shriveling.
immediate_actions: Identify and flag early focal patches ('foci') in the field.
Avoid excessive irrigation during cold, overcast periods.
Report immediate presence to local extension authorities for regional surveillance.
prevention: Grow stripe-rust-resistant wheat cultivars.
Avoid growing highly susceptible legacy varieties in foothills and northern plains.
Practice uniform timely sowing across the village cluster.
monitoring: Scout cool, shaded parts of fields (near trees, canals) during December to February (10-15°C).
Look for yellow linear stripes on lower and middle leaves.
diseases.expert_escalation: Immediately report any stripe rust foci to KVK or District Agriculture Officer for community-wide advisories.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Stem rust (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici) is a late-season rust occurring in warm temperatures, producing large, elongated reddish-brown pustules on stems and leaf sheaths.
symptoms: Large, elongated, dark reddish-brown to blackish pustules on stems, leaf sheaths, and heads.
Pustules rupturing the epidermis, leaving ragged, frayed epidermal tissue around the edges.
Stems becoming brittle and lodging heavily under wind.
Severe grain shriveling and total crop lodging in heavy epidemics.
immediate_actions: Scout stems and leaf sheaths across the entire field for ragged brown pustules.
Avoid late nitrogen applications that prolong vegetative succulence.
Harvest mature fields promptly to avoid pre-harvest lodging losses.
prevention: Plant stem-rust-resistant wheat varieties.
Eradicate alternate barberry hosts if present in proximity to wheat fields.
Sow early to escape late-season warm temperature peaks.
monitoring: Scout stems and leaf sheaths from boot stage through grain maturity under warm weather (>20°C).
Inspect lower stems where initial pustules erupt through the green bark.
diseases.expert_escalation: Immediately notify KVK or agricultural extension officers upon confirmation of stem rust.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Loose smut (Ustilago tritici) is an internally seed-borne fungal disease where entire emergent wheat heads are transformed into masses of black powdery spores.
symptoms: Entire wheat head (spike) converted into a loose, powdery mass of olive-black spores.
Infected heads emerging earlier than healthy heads.
Black spore mass blowing away in the wind, leaving only a bare central rachis (skeleton head).
Normal vegetative growth prior to heading with no visible foliar symptoms.
immediate_actions: Carefully rogue out smutted heads early in the morning into plastic bags before spores disperse.
Burn or bury bagged smutted heads deep in the ground away from wheat fields.
Never save seeds from loose-smut-affected fields for next year's crop.
prevention: Use certified loose-smut-free seed from authorized government seed agencies.
Treat seeds before sowing with hot water or certified systemic fungicidal seed treatments.
Adopt solar seed treatment (soaking seeds in water for 4 hours, then drying in hot summer sun on a tarp).
monitoring: Scout wheat fields daily during the head emergence (earhead emergence) stage.
Look for blackened emergent spikes standing taller than the green canopy.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult KVK for certified seed replacement and solar seed treatment demonstrations.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Karnal bunt (Tilletia indica) is a fungal disease affecting developing wheat grains, converting portions of the grain into a black powdery mass that emits a characteristic foul fishy odor.
symptoms: Only a portion of the grain in an earhead converted into black powdery teliospores (partial bunting).
Embryo end or longitudinal crease of the grain blackened and hollowed.
Characteristic rotten fish odor (due to trimethylamine) in harvested bunted grain.
Infected spikes showing slightly spread-out glumes at maturity.
immediate_actions: Do not use bunted wheat lots as seed for subsequent crop cycles.
Thoroughly clean combine harvesters and grain storage bins after handling bunted lots.
Deep summer plowing to bury teliospores beneath the germination zone.
prevention: Sow certified Karnal-bunt-free seed in disease-free geographical zones.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization and excessive irrigation at the heading stage.
Adopt crop rotation with non-host crops like gram, mustard, or lentil.
monitoring: Scout fields during flowering when temperatures are 18-24°C with overcast skies or light rain.
Inspect threshed grain samples under good light for blackened, fishy-smelling grains.
diseases.expert_escalation: Report Karnal bunt occurrence to district agricultural officers for quarantine and seed certification management.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Red rot (Colletotrichum falcatum) is the most destructive fungal disease of sugarcane ('cancer of sugarcane'), causing internal red discoloration of stalks with white patches and plant drying.
symptoms: Yellowing and drying of upper leaves (third or fourth leaf from top) starting from margins towards the midrib.
Entire crown drying up and whole cane collapsing in the field.
Splitting the stalk reveals longitudinal dark red pith discoloration interspersed with distinct white transverse patches.
Internal pith smelling sour or alcoholic (fermented juice smell).
immediate_actions: Uproot and burn dried, red-rot-affected cane stools along with underground stubble.
Do not take a ratoon crop from fields showing red rot incidence.
Drain stagnant water from the field; do not let irrigation water flow from diseased to healthy fields.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free setts from healthy seed nurseries.
Adopt moist hot air treatment (MHAT at 54°C for 2.5 hours) or hot water treatment of seed setts.
Grow red-rot-resistant sugarcane varieties recommended by local sugar research stations.
monitoring: Scout fields during post-monsoon months (August to November) when red rot symptoms peak.
Split open stalks of unthrifty, yellowing canes to examine the pith.
diseases.expert_escalation: Immediately inform local Sugar Mill cane development officer or KVK if red rot is detected in seed plots.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Sugarcane smut (Sporisorium scitamineum) produces a prominent, curved, whip-like black dusty structure from the terminal shoot of the cane, stunting growth and ruining juice.
symptoms: Emergence of a long, pencil-thick, curved whip-like structure (20-150 cm) from the cane shoot tip.
Whip initially covered by a thin silvery membrane that ruptures to release billions of black sooty spores.
Severe stunting of stools with thin, spindly, grass-like tillers (witches' broom appearance).
Narrow, erect, small leaves on infected stalks.
immediate_actions: Carefully cover smut whips with a damp gunny bag, cut the entire stalk from the base, and burn it.
Never shake or snap dry smut whips in the field to prevent wind dispersal of spores.
Do not ratoon smut-infested cane stools; dig out the root clump entirely.
prevention: Plant certified smut-free seed cane setts.
Treat seed setts in hot water (52°C for 30 minutes) before planting.
Grow smut-resistant sugarcane varieties.
monitoring: Scout fields weekly during formative and tillering stages (2 to 5 months after planting).
Look for emergent shoots exhibiting silver or black terminal whips.
diseases.expert_escalation: Report smut outbreaks to local sugarcane extension officers for community sanitation drives.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Sugarcane wilt (Cephalosporium sacchari / Fusarium sacchari) causes gradual yellowing, drying of the crown, hollow cane stalks, and purple-reddish internal discoloration.
symptoms: Gradual yellowing and withering of leaves starting from the crown during post-monsoon periods.
Cane stalks losing weight, turning light and hollow with boat-shaped internal cavities.
Splitting the cane reveals diffuse reddish-purple pith discoloration without distinct white bands.
Cane juice quantity and sugar recovery severely depressed.
immediate_actions: Harvest wilted stalks promptly and destroy infected stubbles after harvest.
Avoid waterlogging and improve soil drainage across the field.
Avoid root damage from deep inter-cultivation implements during late growth stages.
prevention: Plant healthy setts obtained from disease-free seed crop nurseries.
Treat setts with hot water before planting.
Practice crop rotation with green manure crops (sunnhemp, daincha) or paddy.
monitoring: Scout fields during dry spells following heavy monsoon rains (September to December).
Check stalks for weight loss, shriveling, and hollow central pith.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult local KVK or Sugarcane Breeding Institute extension agronomists for soil health management.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Grassy shoot disease (GSD), caused by phytoplasmas transmitted by aphids and leafhoppers, leads to profuse, thin, chlorotic grass-like tillering without forming normal millable cane stalks.
symptoms: Proliferation of numerous thin, stunted, pencil-thin shoots from the base of the stool (grassy, bushy clump).
Leaves completely yellow, pale cream, or white (albino) with narrow, papery blades.
Failure to form normal millable cane stalks, causing total yield loss in affected clumps.
Severe stunting and yellowing particularly noticeable in ratoon crops.
immediate_actions: Uproot and destroy bushy, grassy clumps immediately to remove phytoplasma inoculum sources.
Do not keep ratoon crops from GSD-infected plant cane fields.
Control vectoring aphid and leafhopper populations around field borders.
prevention: Plant setts derived from hot water treated (50°C for 2 hours) or aerated steam treated (54°C for 1 hour) nurseries.
Use certified tissue-culture-raised sugarcane plantlets.
Rotate with non-host legume or cereal crops.
monitoring: Inspect ratoon sprouts and young plant crops at 1-3 months for bushy, grassy shoots.
Look for pale white or cream-colored young tillers.
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult sugarcane extension scientists for seed nursery certification and heat therapy facilities.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.

diseases.overview: Pokkah boeng (Fusarium moniliforme / Gibberella fujikuroi) is an airborne fungal disease causing malformation, wrinkling, twisting, and chlorosis of young sugarcane spindle leaves during the monsoon.
symptoms: Chlorotic whitening of the base of young emergent spindle leaves.
Wrinkling, twisting, shortening, and bunching of young leaves at the crown (top rot phase).
Reddish-brown ladder-like transverse lesions inside the leaf sheath and stem.
Death of the growing point and stalk rotting in severe acute cases.
immediate_actions: Prune off severely deformed, twisted top spindle leaves during early monsoon breaks.
Ensure field drainage is rapid so high humidity does not linger around cane crowns.
Avoid excess nitrogen top-dressing during heavy monsoon rain spells.
prevention: Plant Pokkah-boeng-tolerant sugarcane varieties.
Treat seed setts with approved biocontrol agents or hot water before planting.
Maintain adequate row spacing for wind circulation across the canopy.
monitoring: Scout fields closely during humid monsoon months (July to September).
Inspect newly emerging whorl leaves for initial base chlorosis and crinkling.
diseases.expert_escalation: Contact sugarcane factory development agronomists if top-rot phase occurs in more than 5% of canes.
diseases.safety_note: Verify symptoms in the field before taking action. Consult local agricultural authorities for region-specific guidance.
